## Book I, Chapter 1: A Long-Expected Pa: Bilbo Baggins celebrates his 111th birthday with a grand party in the Shire, then shocks his neighbors by disappearing using his magic ring and leaving the ring behind for his nephew Frodo. Gandalf oversees the handoff of the ring, pressing Bilbo to relinquish it despite the hobbit's growing reluctance and possessiveness. Frodo inherits Bag End and the mysterious ring, unaware of the danger it carries.
## Book I, Chapter 2: The Shadow of the: Seventeen years after Bilbo's party, Gandalf returns to the Shire and reveals to Frodo that the ring Bilbo left behind is in fact the One Ring forged by the Dark Lord Sauron, and that the terrifying Black Riders—Sauron's Ringwraiths—are already searching for it. Gandalf recounts the history of the Ring and warns that it must be taken away from the Shire immediately to keep both Frodo and the Shire safe. Frodo resolves to leave Bag End, taking the Ring away from his home, and Sam Gamgee is caught eavesdropping and conscripted to accompany his master.
## Book I, Chapter 3: Three Is Company: Frodo, Sam, and Pippin set out from Bag End toward Buckland, traveling through the fields and woods of the Shire while Frodo quietly sells Bag End to the Sackville-Bagginses as cover for his departure. The hobbits have an eerie first encounter with a Black Rider on the road, whose interest in "Baggins" frightens them, though they narrowly avoid detection by ducking into the trees. They are briefly comforted by a company of High Elves led by Gildor, who warns Frodo that the Riders are dangerous but urges him to hasten his journey.
## Book I, Chapter 4: A Short Cut to Mus: The three hobbits cut across fields belonging to Farmer Maggot, whom Frodo has avoided for years after a childhood mushroom-stealing incident, and Maggot reveals that a Black Rider has come to his farm asking for "Baggins." Maggot drives the hobbits in his wagon through the foggy evening toward the Bucklebury Ferry, and the group is briefly terrified by a dark figure on the road that turns out to be Merry waiting to meet them. They cross the Brandywine River by ferry, leaving the Shire and entering Buckland.
## Book I, Chapter 5: A Conspiracy Unmas: Frodo arrives at Crickhollow, a small house in Buckland that serves as a decoy destination, where Merry and Fatty Bolger reveal that they have known about the Ring and Frodo's plan all along and have been secretly preparing to accompany him. Merry, Pippin, and Sam confront Frodo with their knowledge and insist on joining the quest, refusing to be left behind. Fatty Bolger remains at Crickhollow as a decoy while the others plan to slip away through the Old Forest the next morning.
## Book I, Chapter 6: The Old Forest: The hobbits enter the ancient and unsettling Old Forest, where the trees seem to press in on them and the paths shift to steer travelers toward the Withywindle river valley. Merry and Pippin fall into an enchanted sleep and are nearly swallowed by the roots of Old Man Willow, a malicious ancient tree, while Frodo and Sam are helpless to free them. At the last moment, a strange and jovial figure named Tom Bombadil comes singing through the wood and commands the tree to release the hobbits.
## Book I, Chapter 7: In the House of To: Tom Bombadil leads the hobbits to his cozy home, where his wife Goldberry welcomes them and they spend two nights in warmth and safety, listening to Tom's songs and stories. Tom reveals himself to be ancient beyond reckoning, claiming to be the eldest of living things, and he handles the One Ring without any apparent effect, which astonishes and unsettles Frodo. The hobbits rest, have vivid dreams, and learn a few of Tom's songs before departing, refreshed, toward the Barrow-downs.
## Book I, Chapter 8: Fog on the Barrow-: After leaving Tom Bombadil's house, the hobbits are caught by a cold fog on the Barrow-downs and Frodo becomes separated from his friends, who are captured by a malevolent Barrow-wight and placed in a burial mound. Frodo resists the creature's enchantment long enough to call out for Tom Bombadil, who comes immediately and drives away the Barrow-wight with his singing, freeing the other hobbits. Tom gives each hobbit a blade from the barrow's ancient hoard—weapons made by the Men of Westernesse—and sends them on their way toward Bree.
## Book I, Chapter 9: At the Sign of The: The hobbits arrive in Bree and take lodging at the Prancing Pony inn, where Frodo gives his name as "Underhill" to avoid attention, but draws unwanted notice when he accidentally puts on the Ring and vanishes in front of the common room. The innkeeper Barliman Butterbur admits he forgot to send a letter from Gandalf warning Frodo about the Ring's danger. A mysterious, rough-looking Ranger sitting in the corner calls himself Strider and tells Frodo they must talk privately.
## Book I, Chapter 10: Strider: Strider reveals his true name is Aragorn, son of Arathorn, a friend of Gandalf and heir to the ancient line of kings, and he offers to guide the hobbits to Rivendell. Butterbur delivers Gandalf's delayed letter, which confirms that Strider can be trusted and urges Frodo to make haste. The company learns that spies of the enemy are in Bree, and they plan a deceptive departure to throw off pursuit.
## Book I, Chapter 11: A Knife in the Da: The Black Riders attack the Prancing Pony in the night, but the hobbits have moved to Strider's room and survive unharmed. Strider leads the company out of Bree and across the wild lands toward the hill of Weathertop, where they find signs that Gandalf was recently there and fought the Riders. On Weathertop's summit, five Ringwraiths attack in the night and their leader stabs Frodo in the shoulder with a Morgul-knife, leaving a shard that begins slowly poisoning him toward a wraith-like existence.
## Book I, Chapter 12: Flight to the For: The company flees southward toward Rivendell with Frodo growing weaker from the Morgul wound, and they are joined briefly by the Elf lord Glorfindel, who lends Frodo his swift white horse. At the Ford of Bruinen—the crossing into Rivendell's territory—the Black Riders pursue Frodo alone on horseback, but as he crosses the river, a great flood conjured by Elrond and Gandalf sweeps the Riders away. Frodo collapses on the far bank, having barely survived, and loses consciousness.
## Book II, Chapter 1: Many Meetings: Frodo awakens in Rivendell in the care of Elrond, who has removed the Morgul shard and healed the wound, though it took several days. Frodo is joyfully reunited with Gandalf, Bilbo, and then Sam, Merry, and Pippin, and he attends a feast in the Hall of Fire where he glimpses many famous figures. Bilbo and Frodo have a touching reunion, and Bilbo has been living quietly in Rivendell, working on his book and enjoying Elvish company.
## Book II, Chapter 2: The Council of El: Elrond convenes a great council of representatives from across Middle-earth—Elves, Dwarves, Men, and Hobbits—to debate what must be done with the One Ring. Each attendee shares news of their own lands, revealing that Sauron's power is growing everywhere and that keeping or hiding the Ring is not a viable option. After hearing that the Ring cannot be used for good and must be destroyed in the fires of Mount Doom, Frodo volunteers to be the Ring-bearer, and the Fellowship of the Ring is formed.
## Book II, Chapter 3: The Ring Goes Sou: The Fellowship of nine—Frodo, Sam, Merry, Pippin, Gandalf, Aragorn, Boromir, Legolas, and Gimli—departs Rivendell and travels south through the wild lands toward the mountains. Their attempt to cross over the Misty Mountains via the Redhorn Pass is thwarted by a supernatural snowstorm that seems to be driven by Sauron's will, and Boromir advocates turning back. After retreating, Gandalf proposes taking the underground route through the Mines of Moria, a suggestion met with unease but ultimately accepted.
## Book II, Chapter 4: A Journey in the: The Fellowship enters the ancient Dwarf realm of Moria through the Doors of Durin, finding only darkness and the bones of Balin's ill-fated colony inside. Gandalf guides the company through the labyrinthine tunnels, and after resting in Balin's tomb they find the record of the colony's last days before the Dwarves were overwhelmed by Orcs. A horde of Orcs and a Cave-troll attack the chamber, and though the Fellowship fights them off, they must flee deeper into the mine.
## Book II, Chapter 5: The Bridge of Kha: The Fellowship races through the mines pursued by Orcs and a massive, ancient fire-demon known as a Balrog, a creature of shadow and flame that even the Orcs seem to fear. On the narrow Bridge of Khazad-dûm spanning a vast chasm, Gandalf stands alone against the Balrog, breaks the bridge beneath it, and sends the creature plunging into the abyss—but the Balrog's whip catches Gandalf and drags him down as well. The rest of the Fellowship flees the mines in grief and exhaustion, emerging into daylight at the eastern gate.
## Book II, Chapter 6: Lothlórien: The grieving Fellowship enters the golden wood of Lothlórien, the ancient Elf realm of Celeborn and Galadriel, where they are cautiously welcomed by the Elf wardens led by Haldir. The company rests safely in the treetop platforms called flets and eventually makes their way to Caras Galadhon, the city of the Galadhrim. Galadriel and Celeborn receive the Fellowship, and Galadriel silently tests each member, gazing into their hearts.
## Book II, Chapter 7: The Mirror of Gal: Galadriel leads Sam and Frodo to her mirror—a basin of water that can show visions of the past, present, or possible futures. Sam sees a frightening vision of the Shire under some kind of ruin, while Frodo sees the Eye of Sauron and offers Galadriel the Ring. She is sorely tempted but refuses, acknowledging that she has long withstood Sauron's shadow and that to accept the Ring would transform her into something terrible.
## Book II, Chapter 8: Farewell to Lórie: After a month of rest in Lothlórien, the Fellowship prepares to depart by boat down the Anduin river, and Galadriel gives each member a personal gift—most notably a phial of starlight to Frodo and the Elvish rope and other useful goods to the others. The company bids a sorrowful farewell to Galadriel and Celeborn on the western shore, and Galadriel sings a lament as the boats drift south. The Fellowship rows away into an uncertain future with renewed resolve.
## Book II, Chapter 9: The Great River: The Fellowship travels southward down the Anduin in their boats, passing through increasingly dangerous and watched lands. Legolas shoots down a large winged creature carrying a spy in the night, and the company is aware that they are being followed and observed. As they approach the Falls of Rauros and the statue-guarded entrance to Gondor's territory, they must decide whether to pass west into Gondor with Boromir or east toward Mordor.
## Book II, Chapter 10: The Breaking of: The Fellowship lands at Amon Hen and Frodo walks apart to think, during which Boromir confronts him and tries to take the Ring by force, driven mad by its influence. Frodo puts on the Ring and flees, sitting alone at the high seat of Amon Hen and briefly glimpsing the Eye of Sauron before Gandalf's spirit seems to help him resist. Frodo decides he must go to Mordor alone to prevent the Ring from corrupting anyone else, but Sam realizes what is happening and refuses to be left behind, wading into the river to join Frodo as they paddle away.
## Book III, Chapter 1: The Departure of: Aragorn finds Boromir sitting against a tree, mortally wounded by many Orc arrows—he died defending Merry and Pippin, who have been captured by the attacking Uruk-hai. Boromir confesses to Aragorn that he tried to take the Ring from Frodo and expresses regret, and Aragorn assures him he has done enough before Boromir dies. Aragorn, Legolas, and Gimli give Boromir a funeral on the river by placing him in one of the boats and letting it go over the falls, then vow to hunt down the Orcs and rescue Merry and Pippin.
## Book III, Chapter 2: The Riders of Ro: Aragorn, Legolas, and Gimli run tirelessly across the plains of Rohan following the trail of the Uruk-hai, hoping to rescue Merry and Pippin before the Orcs reach Isengard. They encounter a company of Rohirrim riders led by Éomer, the nephew of King Théoden, who tells them that the Rohirrim have already slain the entire Orc band in the night with no sign of any hobbits surviving. Éomer lends them horses and rides on, while the three companions arrive at the edge of Fangorn Forest, where recent signs suggest the hobbits may have entered.
## Book III, Chapter 3: The Uruk-hai: This chapter follows Merry and Pippin from the time of their capture, as the Uruk-hai of Saruman and the Orcs of Mordor clash over which master the hobbits should be brought to, with the Uruks killing those who would take them to Sauron. During a night halt on the plains, Grishnákh—an Orc from Mordor—tries to steal the hobbits for the Ring, but is killed by Rohirrim cavalry in the surprise attack. In the chaos of the battle, Merry and Pippin manage to escape their bonds and flee into Fangorn Forest.
## Book III, Chapter 4: Treebeard: Merry and Pippin encounter Treebeard, an ancient Ent—a giant tree-herder who tends the trees of Fangorn—who speaks slowly but with great wisdom and carries the hobbits to his home at Wellinghall. Treebeard is angered to learn what Saruman has been doing, cutting down trees without thought or mercy and building armies of destruction. He calls an Entmoot—a great gathering of Ents—to debate what action they should take.
## Book III, Chapter 5: The White Rider: Aragorn, Legolas, and Gimli track the hobbits' trail into Fangorn and instead encounter an old man in white robes whom they at first take for Saruman and attack. The figure reveals himself to be Gandalf, returned from his fall into the abyss after his battle with the Balrog—he has been sent back as Gandalf the White, now more powerful than before. Gandalf shares news of the wider war and tells them they must ride to Rohan, where King Théoden is under Saruman's dark influence.
## Book III, Chapter 6: The King of the: Gandalf, Aragorn, Legolas, and Gimli arrive at Edoras, the great hall of Rohan, and force their way to King Théoden despite the opposition of Gríma Wormtongue, Saruman's spy in the king's court. Gandalf confronts the withered, enchanted king and breaks Saruman's hold over him, restoring Théoden to his strength and rightful authority. Théoden expels Gríma, who flees to Isengard, and resolves to ride to war and defend Rohan against Saruman's forces.
## Book III, Chapter 7: Helm's Deep: Théoden leads the people of Edoras to the ancient fortress of Helm's Deep as Saruman's vast army of Uruk-hai marches against them, and through the night the defenders hold the walls against overwhelming numbers. The enemy breaks through the outer gate using a blasting fire, and the defenders fall back to the inner keep, seemingly on the verge of defeat as dawn approaches. At first light, Gandalf arrives with Éomer and a fresh cavalry force, the Huorns of Fangorn come up from behind to destroy the Orc army, and the enemy is routed.
## Book III, Chapter 8: The Road to Isen: Théoden and his Riders, along with Gandalf and the companions, ride toward Isengard to confront Saruman, passing through a landscape where the Huorns have herded and destroyed the remaining Orcs. They arrive at the gates of Isengard to find it utterly destroyed—the great fortress is flooded and in ruins, with Orthanc's tower standing alone in the wreckage. To their astonishment, Merry and Pippin are found sitting comfortably on the rubble, eating and drinking the stores they found in Saruman's larder.
## Book III, Chapter 9: Flotsam and Jets: Merry and Pippin recount the story of the Entmoot to Aragorn, Gandalf, and the others—how the Ents eventually decided to march to war and broke open Isengard in a single furious assault, flooding it with water from the diverted river. The hobbits share their finds of Longbottom Leaf pipe-weed from Saruman's store, which puzzles Gandalf. The company also discovers that a supply chain of goods from the Shire had been passing through Isengard, hinting at Saruman's deeper schemes.
## Book III, Chapter 10: The Voice of Sa: Gandalf leads the company to Orthanc tower to parlay with Saruman, who speaks from a high window with his enchanting, persuasive voice, trying to sway each listener to his side. Gandalf breaks Saruman's staff and casts him from the order, declaring him expelled and powerless, while Saruman retreats in impotent fury. Gríma hurls a heavy palantír stone from the tower in a rage, which Pippin recovers from the ground—a seemingly trivial act with great consequences.
## Book III, Chapter 11: The Palantír: The stone Gríma threw is revealed to be a palantír—one of the ancient seeing-stones that can be used to communicate and view distant events—and in the night Pippin cannot resist looking into it, accidentally making contact with Sauron himself. Sauron mistakes Pippin for the Ring-bearer and Pippin is wracked by a terrible vision, though no vital information about the Ring is revealed. Gandalf, alarmed, resolves to ride immediately with Pippin to Minas Tirith, the capital of Gondor, to warn them and keep Pippin from further danger.
## Book IV, Chapter 1: The Taming of Smé: Frodo and Sam, having crossed the Emyn Muil alone, realize they are being followed by Gollum—who has tracked the Ring from Mordor all the way to the Fellowship. Frodo surprises and subdues Gollum with the help of Sam and the Elvish rope, which burns Gollum's skin painfully, and Frodo promises not to hurt him if he will serve as guide to Mordor. Despite Sam's deep distrust, Frodo extends a kind of pity to Gollum, calling him Sméagol and forming a wary alliance.
## Book IV, Chapter 2: The Passage of th: Gollum leads Frodo and Sam across the treacherous Dead Marshes—vast bogs full of the ancient dead whose corpse-candle lights lure travelers to their doom. Frodo nearly drowns when drawn to look at the faces below the water, and Sam pulls him back. They survive the crossing and approach the desolate wasteland before the Black Gate of Mordor.
## Book IV, Chapter 3: The Black Gate Is: The three arrive at the Morannon—the great Black Gate of Mordor—and find it massively guarded and entirely impassable for a small group. Gollum pleads with them not to enter that way and promises to show them a secret pass into Mordor—Cirith Ungol—which Frodo eventually agrees to try despite Sam's suspicion that Gollum is leading them into a trap. They hide from an army of Easterlings who march in through the gate and then turn south toward Ithilien.
## Book IV, Chapter 4: Of Herbs and Stew: The trio travels through Ithilien, the ruined but still-beautiful land east of the Anduin, and Frodo and Sam experience a moment of peace as Sam cooks a meal with herbs and the rabbits Gollum has caught. A company of Men—Rangers of Gondor led by Faramir, the younger son of Denethor—suddenly surrounds them, as the Men have ambushed a Haradrim force marching to Mordor. Faramir takes Frodo and Sam captive for questioning, regarding them with suspicion but also with surprising courtesy.
## Book IV, Chapter 5: The Window on the: Faramir leads Frodo and Sam to a hidden refuge behind a waterfall called Henneth Annûn, where he questions Frodo carefully about his mission and Boromir's death. Frodo speaks truthfully about much but conceals the nature of the Ring, and Faramir reveals that he already knows something of Isildur's Bane—the One Ring—from Boromir's dream. Faramir explicitly refuses to take the Ring even if he found it on the road, demonstrating the moral fortitude that distinguishes him from his brother.
## Book IV, Chapter 6: The Forbidden Poo: In the night, Faramir wakes Frodo to show him Gollum fishing in the forbidden pool below Henneth Annûn—a place where any trespasser must be killed by the laws of the Rangers. Frodo must call Gollum to him to prevent the Rangers from killing him, which he does, though it strains the trust between Sméagol and Frodo since Gollum feels trapped and betrayed by being led into an ambush. Faramir captures Gollum and questions him, then releases him into Frodo's custody and warns Frodo that Gollum is leading them to danger.
## Book IV, Chapter 7: Journey to the Cr: Faramir escorts Frodo and Sam to the edge of Ithilien, gives them food and supplies, and warns them that Cirith Ungol is a place of great evil that has not been used in many years, urging them to find another way. The hobbits and Gollum reach the ancient Cross-roads—a stone circle where roads from several directions meet—and see the defaced statue of a king with a wreath of wildflowers placed on it by someone unknown. They head up the road toward Minas Morgul as the sky darkens with an unnatural storm.
## Book IV, Chapter 8: The Stairs of Cir: The three approach Minas Morgul—the tower of the Ringwraiths, once Minas Ithil—and Frodo is nearly overwhelmed by the Ring's call as a great army led by the Lord of the Nazgûl marches out of the gates below them, signaling that the war has begun. They climb the winding Straight Stair and then the more treacherous Winding Stair carved into the cliffs of Cirith Ungol, ascending thousands of feet toward the pass. At the top of the stairs they find a small sheltered cleft, and while Gollum thinks the hobbits are asleep he is overheard by Sam having an argument with himself about whether to help them or betray them to Shelob.
## Book IV, Chapter 9: Shelob's Lair: Gollum leads Frodo and Sam through the dark tunnels of Torech Ungol—the lair of Shelob, a monstrous ancient spider—and then abandons them to the creature, having arranged for Shelob to kill them so he can recover the Ring from her refuse. Sam fights off a first attack using the Elvish rope, and Frodo uses the Phial of Galadriel to drive Shelob back, but the creature circles and stings Frodo from behind, paralyzing him. Sam arrives too late to protect Frodo, drives Shelob off with the Phial and the sword Sting, and is left alone with what he believes to be Frodo's corpse.
## Book IV, Chapter 10: The Choices of M: Sam, in his grief, must decide whether to leave Frodo behind or take the Ring himself to continue the mission, and after agonizing deliberation he takes the Ring and begins to climb toward the tunnel exit. He spots Gollum and nearly attacks him, then reaches the gate of Cirith Ungol only to see a company of Orcs emerge and carry Frodo's body inside—he realizes Frodo is not dead but paralyzed by the spider's venom. Sam cannot follow before the iron gate clangs shut, and he is left outside the tower, alone with the Ring and the desperate need to rescue his master.
## Book V, Chapter 1: Minas Tirith: Gandalf rides with Pippin on Shadowfax at great speed from Isengard to Minas Tirith, the city of Gondor, arriving before the war begins and bringing Pippin who pledges his service to Denethor, the Steward of Gondor. Pippin is set to serve in the Guard of the Citadel, and he explores the great seven-tiered city while Gandalf meets with Denethor, whose grief over Boromir's death has made him bitter and obstinate. The city begins to prepare for siege, and Faramir arrives to report on his encounter with Frodo—news that both saddens and angers Denethor.
## Book V, Chapter 2: The Passing of the: A company of Rangers of the North—kinsmen of Aragorn—arrives at Helm's Deep, led by Halbarad and including Elladan and Elrohir, the sons of Elrond, bearing a standard for Aragorn from Arwen. Aragorn is troubled by visions in the palantír he has dared to use, and he decides to take the Paths of the Dead—a haunted road through the mountain that no living man dares travel—to summon the army of the Dead who are oath-bound to serve the heir of Isildur. Aragorn departs from Dunharrow with the Grey Company while Théoden leads the main Rohirrim army by the regular road toward Gondor.
## Book V, Chapter 3: The Muster of Roha: This chapter follows Merry and Éowyn as they ride with the mustering Rohirrim to Dunharrow, the great mountain fortress where Théoden's host assembles. A stranger named Dernhelm—whom Merry later realizes is Éowyn in disguise—offers to carry Merry on her horse since Théoden has forbidden the hobbit to ride to battle. The Rohirrim set out from Dunharrow along a secret road toward Gondor, and a dark shadow of Sauron's power eclipses the sun as they ride.
## Book V, Chapter 4: The Siege of Gondo: Sauron's vast army pours out of Mordor and lays siege to Minas Tirith, overwhelming the outer defenses and burning the lower levels of the city while Denethor retreats into despair. Faramir is gravely wounded in a rearguard action and is brought back near death, which breaks Denethor's will entirely—he sinks into madness, convinced that Sauron cannot be defeated. The Lord of the Nazgûl uses a great black mace to break the ancient city gates, and the first wall of the city falls.
## Book V, Chapter 5: The Ride of the Ro: The Rohirrim arrive on the Pelennor Fields outside Minas Tirith at dawn, and Théoden rallies his riders for a great charge against the besieging army. The Rohirrim crash into Sauron's forces, shattering the siege lines and driving the enemy back, and Théoden himself rides in glory at the head of the charge. The Lord of the Nazgûl flies down on his winged beast and attacks the king, mortally wounding Théoden's horse and crushing the king beneath it.
## Book V, Chapter 6: The Battle of the: Éowyn, revealed to be the disguised Rohirrim warrior, stands over the fallen king and faces the Lord of the Nazgûl, who declares that no living man can slay him—to which she replies that she is no man, then kills the creature and wounds the Nazgûl lord, who is then finished by Merry's ancient Barrow-blade. The Corsairs of Umbar arrive at the river but the ships are taken by Aragorn, who has come up from the south with the army of the Dead that has now fulfilled its oath, followed by new reinforcements. The battle turns entirely against Sauron and the fields are eventually cleared, though at great cost including the death of Théoden.
## Book V, Chapter 7: The Pyre of Deneth: Denethor, mad with grief over Faramir's seemingly fatal wound and convinced all is lost, commands his servants to build a great funeral pyre and burn both himself and Faramir alive in the tombs of Rath Dínen. Pippin, horrified, summons Gandalf and they race to the tombs, arriving just in time for Gandalf to rescue Faramir—who is not dead—while Denethor leaps onto the pyre himself and burns, clutching a palantír whose visions of Sauron's power had destroyed his hope. Faramir is rescued and the steward's line of authority passes to him, though he remains unconscious.
## Book V, Chapter 8: The Houses of Heal: In the aftermath of the battle, the wounded—including Faramir, Éowyn, and Merry—are brought to the Houses of Healing in Minas Tirith, where they lie in a dangerous swoon that healers cannot cure. An ancient lore holds that the hands of the king bring healing, and Aragorn, prompted by Gandalf, comes in disguise to the Houses and uses a herb called athelas to wake the three from their near-death states. Aragorn's healing confirms his royal lineage to those who witness it, though he continues to keep his full identity quiet for the moment.
## Book V, Chapter 9: The Last Debate: Aragorn, Gandalf, and the other leaders of the West meet to debate their next move, knowing their army is too small to take Mordor by force but aware that they must do something to draw Sauron's attention away from Frodo. Gandalf proposes marching all available forces to the Black Gate as a feint—to challenge Sauron directly and force him to look outward, giving Frodo a chance to complete the quest even though it will almost certainly mean the army's destruction. The commanders agree to this desperate strategy, and a final force is assembled to march on the Morannon.
## Book V, Chapter 10: The Black Gate Op: Aragorn leads the combined army of the West to the Black Gate and sends a herald to challenge Sauron, demanding his surrender and the release of all prisoners. The Mouth of Sauron rides out to negotiate, bringing Frodo's mithril coat, Elvish rope, and Sam's cooking gear as proof that the Ring-bearer has been captured, though this is a bluff. When Aragorn refuses to yield and the parlay breaks down, the gates open and a great host pours out to overwhelm them—at which point the Nazgûl fly overhead, the army of the West is surrounded, and the battle seems utterly lost.
## Book VI, Chapter 1: The Tower of Ciri: Sam, carrying the Ring, finds a way into the tower of Cirith Ungol and discovers that the Orc garrison has been devastated by an internal battle between two factions fighting over Frodo's mithril coat. He uses the Phial of Galadriel and his own courage to make his way to the top of the tower, where he finds Frodo alive but naked, having been stripped and interrogated. Sam returns the Ring to Frodo and they disguise themselves in Orc clothing to escape, slipping out of the tower and into Mordor.
## Book VI, Chapter 2: The Land of Shado: Frodo and Sam travel through the blasted, ash-covered wastes of Mordor, joining a column of Orc soldiers at one point to avoid detection before slipping away. The Ring grows heavier with every step as they draw closer to Mount Doom, and Frodo becomes barely able to walk under its spiritual weight. Gollum reappears and assaults Frodo, trying to take the Ring, but is driven off by Sam.
## Book VI, Chapter 3: Mount Doom: Frodo and Sam reach the Sammath Naur—the Crack of Doom inside Mount Doom—after Sam carries Frodo up the final slopes, but at the edge of the Fire Frodo refuses to destroy the Ring, instead claiming it as his own and putting it on. Gollum attacks the invisible Frodo, bites off his finger and reclaims the Ring in ecstasy, then dances on the edge of the chasm and falls in—taking the Ring with him into the fire and destroying it. The moment the Ring is destroyed, Sauron's tower and armies collapse, the Nazgûl are annihilated, and Frodo and Sam are left stranded on the slopes as the mountain erupts.
## Book VI, Chapter 4: The Field of Corm: Gandalf sends the great Eagles to rescue Frodo and Sam from the slopes of Mount Doom before the eruption engulfs them, and they are brought to safety and allowed to sleep and recover. They awake in Ithilien at the Field of Cormallen, where the army of the West has gathered in celebration, and are brought before Aragorn surrounded by cheering Men, Elves, and Dwarves. A minstrel is called to sing the praise of the Ring-bearers before the whole host.
## Book VI, Chapter 5: The Steward and t: The company returns to Minas Tirith, where Faramir formally yields his authority as Steward and offers the ancient crown of the kings of Gondor to Aragorn. Aragorn is crowned King Elessar of Gondor and Arnor, and he begins to restore the city and the kingdom, establishing justice and beginning the long work of healing. Aragorn's first sight of Arwen, who arrives with Elrond and a company of Elves, fulfills the long-deferred promise of their love, and Elrond gives his blessing for them to wed.
## Book VI, Chapter 6: Many Partings: The great company of friends begins to break apart as each goes their own way—Éomer takes Théoden's body back to Rohan for burial, and the hobbits and their companions travel with Aragorn and Arwen for a time before parting. Treebeard is met in Fangorn and bids farewell to Celeborn and Galadriel, and Saruman is encountered on the road—thin, ragged, and bitter—and refuses Gandalf's offer of aid. Saruman hints darkly to the hobbits that something unpleasant awaits them in the Shire.
## Book VI, Chapter 7: Homeward Bound: The hobbits and Gandalf travel northward toward the Shire, stopping at Rivendell for a time where Frodo finds Bilbo—now 131 years old, frail, and dozing—who has almost forgotten the Ring and seems at peace. Gandalf parts from the hobbits at the edge of the Shire, telling them they must deal with whatever lies ahead themselves and that they have strength enough to do it after all they have experienced. The hobbits ride on alone into the Shire, expecting a cheerful homecoming.
## Book VI, Chapter 8: The Scouring of t: The hobbits return to find the Shire occupied and ruined—trees felled, buildings torn down, and the people oppressed by Ruffians under the orders of a mysterious figure called Sharkey, who turns out to be Saruman himself. Merry and Pippin organize a hobbit rebellion and defeat the Ruffians, but Saruman confronts them at Bag End with murderous spite before Gríma finally snaps and kills him, then is shot down by hobbit archers. The Shire is freed, but much is destroyed and will take years to restore—Frodo finds that even in victory the wounds of the quest have not fully healed.
## Book VI, Chapter 9: The Grey Havens: Sam uses the gift from Galadriel—a box of Elvish earth and a mallorn seed—to help restore the Shire, and the land heals remarkably in the following year. Frodo, however, remains wounded in spirit and body; though he married no one and found no peace, Sam weds Rose Cotton and settles into a full hobbit life. On September 22nd, Frodo, Bilbo, and Gandalf ride to the Grey Havens where Galadriel, Celeborn, and Elrond also await—and Frodo, as a Ring-bearer, is granted passage to the Undying Lands across the sea, leaving a grieving Sam behind to live on in the Shire with the life he has made.
